mutations.label: a declaration that asks for object storage no longer gets it, so the stack's bucket falls to `count = 0` and the conformance leg passes while proving nothing about local storage — which is exactly the failure mode the inventory assertion in stacks.sh exists to make impossible

object storage is armed for EVERY declaration, so `feint up` writes bytes on the disk of a reader who never mentioned one. The silent half of the same guard, and the one a careless fix would break: `runtime.mode` is absent by default for this very reason

the declared doors stop reaching the command line, so the emulator serves the CLI's default list and the stack's ch-dk-2 bucket lands on a prefix nobody mounted. A 404 there reads as a broken emulator rather than as a door that was asked for and dropped

note:
The subject is #850's criterion that an Exoscale SOS-dependent stack reach LOCAL object storage, and the pieces `up` needed for it: a `storage.*` block in feint.yaml, armed only when asked.

Why the second mutation matters as much as the first. Writing bytes is a side effect on the operator's disk, which is why `storage.directory` is absent by default exactly as `runtime.mode` is — a fix that armed storage unconditionally would make `feint up` create a byte store for a reader who never mentioned one. The guard has two directions and a mutation for each.

Measured on the way here, and both findings are in docs/limits.md rather than only in a commit message. The Exoscale provider has NO bucket resource (0.72.0: its only storage resource is `exoscale_sos_bucket_policy`, which does not create a bucket and whose three verbs this emulator answers 501), so the bucket goes through the AWS provider pointed at `sos_endpoint` — which is what Exoscale users write. And there is no `aws_s3_object` beside it: the object applies and its bytes land locally, sha256 identical, but every later plan wants to update it in place because it compares the ETag a read returns against `filemd5` and this emulator returns none, on PUT, HEAD and GET alike. Serving an MD5 would mean a v5 byte format older binaries could not read, and a permanent diff in an example teaches a reader that drift is normal here.

Two guards here are asserted and NOT falsified, for the reason recorded in hardcoded-endpoint-row-is-owned.json: the harness requires every name in `find` to survive into `replace`, and neither a door list in a shell script nor a YAML endpoint can satisfy that. They are TestEveryDeclaredStorageEndpointNamesADeclaredDoor, which joins `storage.doors` to the `iac.vars` endpoint, and the door-list parity across the three conformance starters. The inventory assertion in stacks.sh WAS proved to bite by hand: with its variable emptied, the leg fails naming the door it looked in.

What the CI run then taught, and it was a population error of exactly the kind CLAUDE.md names. The first version exported TF_VAR_sos_endpoint unconditionally, so the `image` job — which runs the shipped container with NO override and therefore serves no door — failed its apply: the stack asked for a bucket on a prefix nobody mounted. Eprouve on the richest run, broken by the poorest. stacks.sh now asks the emulator which doors it serves (GET /_feint/s3) and decides from that, which is this repository's own rule: branch on a declaration, never on a name you expect.

And the decision is recorded in SOS_DOOR rather than inferred from the variable, because an assertion keyed off its own input cannot report the bug where that input went missing (#459, a suite skipping itself). Three executions were measured by hand: no door at all (a note, verdict 0), three doors (the assertion holds, verdict 0), and a served door with the export emptied (the leg FAILS, naming the door it looked in). The third is the one that proves the guard cannot skip itself.
